case_analysis.focal_point: Whether venue for a prosecution under 18 U.S.C. § 1519 is proper in the judicial district where the contemplated/targeted federal investigation was located, even if the defendant’s alleged falsification or destruction of records occurred entirely in another district.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (Sarbanes–Oxley anti-shredding/falsification statute) and Article III, § 2, cl. 3 plus the Sixth Amendment Vicinage/Venue guarantees (as implemented through federal venue doctrine).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues venue is improper where no conduct elements of the § 1519 offense occurred, and that allowing prosecution in the district of the investigation based merely on § 1519’s intent-to-obstruct language (i.e., effects that might be contemplated there) converts venue into an effects/foreseeability test untethered to where the crime was committed; under Supreme Court venue precedents, venue must be based on where the statute’s essential conduct elements occurred, and § 1519’s mens rea/intent element cannot by itself supply venue in a district with no relevant acts. Petitioner’s amici (e.g., Cato, NACDL/NAFD) frame this as a structural constitutional issue that invites forum shopping and dilutes the vicinage right by letting the government pick a favorable district simply because an investigation is located there.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues venue is proper in the district of the federal investigation at which the obstructive conduct was directed because § 1519 criminalizes falsification/destruction of records done with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence an investigation or proper administration of a matter within federal jurisdiction; when a statute defines the offense in terms of obstructive conduct aimed at an investigation, the place where that investigation is situated is a proper venue since the offense is functionally ‘directed at’ and felt in that district. In the government’s view, trying the case where the affected federal proceeding/investigation is located fits § 1519’s design and avoids artificial venue limitations that would disconnect obstruction prosecutions from the locus of the investigation being obstructed.
key_precedents: Ciminelli v. United States, 598 U.S. 306 (2023) (right-to-control theory rejected)
United States v. Kellington, 217 F.3d 1084 (9th Cir. 2000)
United States v. Alston, 974 F.2d 1206 (9th Cir. 1992)
United States v. Del Toro-Barboza, 673 F.3d 1136 (9th Cir. 2012)
United States v. Camacho, 555 F.3d 695 (8th Cir. 2009)
United States v. Rafiekian, 991 F.3d 529 (4th Cir. 2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with Petitioner because the government’s best point—that § 1519 is obstructionary and thus venue should follow the investigation’s location—would convert venue into an effects/foreseeability test even though § 1519 requires no pending investigation and no successful obstruction. Justice Thomas persuasively grounds the analysis in Rodriguez-Moreno’s essential-conduct-element framework: the only proscribed conduct is falsifying/destroying/concealing records, while the federal-matter and intent language are mens rea/circumstance features that cannot, under Cabrales, relocate venue to a district where none of the defendant’s acts occurred. Justice Kagan’s institutional concern is also right: absent a clear congressional venue rule, anchoring venue to wherever agents sit invites forum shopping and weakens Article III/Sixth Amendment vicinage protections. I would keep our holding narrow—limited to § 1519 on these facts—leaving Congress free to specify broader venue if it wishes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that § 1519 is obstructionary and so venue should lie where the federal investigation sits, but that collapses constitutional venue into an effects-based theory that the Sixth Amendment and Article III do not permit absent clear statutory text. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 1519 contains no venue clause, so Anderson and Rodriguez-Moreno require locating venue by the statute’s essential conduct elements; those are the verbs “falsifies,” “destroys,” “mutilates,” “conceals,” etc., all of which occurred outside the charging district. Cabrales confirms that circumstance or downstream-proceeding locations cannot substitute for where the prohibited acts were committed, and (as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch note) § 1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” language supplies mens rea/context, not additional conduct that can relocate venue. Accepting the government’s view would let prosecutors pick a forum based on where agents choose to investigate, untethering venue from the place of commission and weakening the vicinage guarantee.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that § 1519 is obstruction-focused and thus venue should follow the locus of the federal matter or investigation, but that theory improperly converts venue into an effects/foreseeability inquiry untethered to the defendant’s acts—precisely what Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno caution against when the charged district contains none of the statute’s essential conduct. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, § 1519 lacks a venue clause, so we must locate the offense by its conduct elements—falsifying, destroying, concealing—which occurred entirely outside the charging district; the “intent to impede” and “in relation to/within federal jurisdiction” language is mens rea/circumstance, not conduct that relocates the locus delicti. Justice Thomas’s observation that § 1519 requires neither a pending investigation nor a successful obstruction further undermines venue pegged to where investigators sit, because the situs could be unknown or shifting at the time of the act. On practical consequences, an investigation-based venue rule invites forum shopping and dilutes Article III/Sixth Amendment vicinage protections absent a clear congressional directive.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The best respondent theory—venue where the federal investigation sits—rests on treating § 1519 as effects-based obstruction, but that collapses Article III and Sixth Amendment venue into foreseeability even though § 1519 requires neither a pending investigation nor any successful obstruction. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan correctly apply Rodriguez-Moreno/Cabrales: the essential conduct elements are the operative verbs (falsify/destroy/conceal), and the “in relation to or contemplation of” and “intent to impede” language is mens rea/circumstance that cannot, by itself, relocate venue to a district where the defendant performed no proscribed acts. Justice Thomas’s point that § 1519 lacks a venue provision reinforces that we should not infer a roving venue rule that enables forum shopping and disproportionately burdens defendants least able to litigate far from home. Under a pragmatic lens attentive to real-world consequences, keeping venue tied to where the acts occurred best protects fairness and access to justice without foreclosing Congress from authorizing broader venue expressly.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that §1519 is obstruction-adjacent and thus venue should lie where the federal matter/investigation is centered because that is where the harm is aimed, but that theory treats intended effects (or a circumstance about a federal matter) as an “act” for locus delicti purposes. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress, Rodriguez-Moreno and Cabrales require anchoring venue to the statute’s essential conduct elements; here the only conduct Congress proscribed is “falsifies,” “destroys,” “conceals,” etc., while the “intent to impede” and “in relation to or contemplation of” phrases are mens rea/circumstance features that cannot relocate venue to a district where no proscribed act occurred. Pragmatically, tying venue to an investigation’s situs—often unknown, movable, or chosen by the Government—invites forum shopping and erodes Article III/Sixth Amendment vicinage protections absent a clear congressional venue directive. No colleague has offered a precedent that permits venue based solely on intent directed at a distant proceeding without any conduct in the charging district, so my position remains that venue lies where the falsification/destruction/concealment occurred.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The government’s best point is that § 1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” language conceptually links the crime to the federal matter’s district, but that asks us to treat a circumstance/mens rea feature as if it were an “essential conduct element” for venue purposes. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Rodriguez-Moreno and Anderson require us to locate the offense by the statute’s conduct verbs—falsifies, destroys, conceals—which occurred outside the charging district; Cabrales likewise warns against anchoring venue in a district where none of the proscribed acts took place. Because § 1519 does not require a pending investigation or any successful obstruction, an effects- or investigation-situs venue theory would untether venue from where the crime was “committed” and invite the forum shopping that the Article III/Sixth Amendment vicinage guarantees are meant to prevent. No colleague has offered a precedent treating intent aimed at a distant federal matter, without any conduct there, as sufficient to establish venue, so I remain with petitioner.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The government’s best point remains that § 1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” federal matter language should allow venue where the investigation sits, but under Rodriguez-Moreno and Cabrales that is a circumstance/mens rea feature, not an essential conduct element that can establish locus delicti in a district where the defendant did nothing. Chief Justice Roberts’s focus on Anderson’s “location of the act or acts constituting” the offense fits our settled venue framework and avoids converting § 1519 into an effects-based venue statute without a clear congressional directive. Justice Thomas’s observation that § 1519 requires neither a pending investigation nor any successful obstruction underscores why tethering venue to an investigation’s situs would invite foreseeability-based forum shopping and dilute Article III/Sixth Amendment vicinage protections. No colleague has supplied contrary precedent treating intent directed at a distant proceeding as sufficient for venue absent any proscribed conduct there, so I remain with petitioner.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The government’s best point is that § 1519 is obstruction-adjacent and should allow venue where the contemplated federal matter is centered, but that treats intended effects or a circumstance element as if it were conduct. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress, Rodriguez-Moreno and Cabrales require us to anchor venue in the statute’s essential conduct elements, and § 1519’s operative verbs—falsifies, destroys, conceals—are the only acts that constitute the offense; the “intent to impede” and “in relation to or contemplation of” language supplies mens rea/context and cannot relocate the locus delicti to a district where no proscribed act occurred. Because § 1519 does not require a pending investigation or any successful obstruction, pegging venue to the investigation’s situs would create an effects/foreseeability regime that Article III and the Sixth Amendment do not permit absent a clear congressional venue directive. I therefore remain with petitioner that venue lies where the falsification/destruction/concealment occurred.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that § 1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” and “intent to impede” language ties the offense to the district of the federal matter—still treats a circumstance/mens rea component as if it were conduct, which our venue cases do not allow absent an express statutory directive. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas correctly anchor the analysis in Rodriguez-Moreno/Cabrales: the essential conduct here is falsifying/destroying/concealing records, and trying the case in a district where none of that conduct occurred would effectively convert venue into an effects/foreseeability test. As Justice Sotomayor emphasizes, that move has concrete fairness costs—forum-shopping incentives and heavier burdens on resource-constrained defendants—undermining the structural vicinage protection the Constitution guarantees. No colleague (and no precedent identified) compels an effects-based venue rule for § 1519, especially given the statute’s lack of any requirement that a federal investigation be pending or that obstruction succeed.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1519 contains no venue provision, so Article III and the Sixth Amendment require venue to be set by the locus delicti—“the location of the act or acts constituting” the offense. United States v. Anderson, 328 U.S. 699, 703 (1946). Under Rodriguez-Moreno’s framework, we look to the statute’s “essential conduct elements” rather than circumstance or mens rea elements, and § 1519’s conduct is the falsification/destruction/concealment of records; the existence or location of a contemplated federal investigation is, at most, a circumstance element and cannot alone supply venue in a district where no relevant acts occurred. A narrow holding to that effect respects precedent, avoids effects-based forum shopping that would erode vicinage protections, and leaves Congress free to enact an explicit venue rule if it wishes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III, § 2, cl. 3 and the Sixth Amendment fix venue where the crime was "committed," which requires identifying § 1519’s essential conduct elements and locating where that conduct occurred. The text of § 1519 criminalizes the act of falsifying, altering, or destroying records; its reference to an investigation is part of the mens rea (“in relation to or contemplation of” and “with the intent to impede”), not an element requiring effects or a nexus to the investigation’s district. Under Cabrales, venue cannot rest on the location of related proceedings or anticipated effects when no essential conduct occurred there; allowing prosecution where the investigation sits would convert venue into an effects/foreseeability test untethered to the place of the defendant’s acts. Because all alleged falsification/destruction occurred in another district, venue in the investigation’s district is improper absent a statutory text making the obstructive conduct a continuing offense reaching that district.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1519 contains no special venue provision, so Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require venue at the locus delicti—“the location of the act or acts constituting” the offense. Anderson, 328 U.S. at 703. Under Rodriguez-Moreno, venue turns on the statute’s “essential conduct elements,” not on circumstance elements or effects; here, the conduct elements are the falsification/destruction/concealment of records, which occurred entirely in the other district, while the “within the jurisdiction of” and intent-to-impede language do not by themselves relocate the crime for venue purposes. 526 U.S. at 279–80 & n.4. Allowing prosecution wherever the investigation happens to be located would untether venue from conduct, invite prosecutorial forum shopping, and dilute the Vicinage guarantee in precisely the way the Constitution’s venue protections were designed to prevent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require venue where the crime was committed, and under this Court’s framework venue turns on the statute’s essential conduct elements and where that conduct occurred. Section 1519’s essential conduct is the act of falsifying, destroying, or concealing records; the intent to impede an investigation is a mens rea element, and (as in Cabrales) related proceedings or contemplated effects in another district cannot supply venue when no conduct element occurred there. Because § 1519 does not require that any investigation be pending or that any obstructive effect actually occur, trying the case in the investigation’s district would convert venue into an effects/foreseeability rule untethered to the locus of criminal conduct, inviting forum shopping and diluting vicinage protections for defendants with fewer resources. Venue therefore lies where the records were falsified or destroyed, not merely where a federal investigation was located.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1519 contains no special venue provision, so venue must be determined by identifying the statute’s “essential conduct elements” and locating where that conduct occurred. Rodriguez-Moreno instructs that inquiry, and Cabrales confirms that venue cannot rest on the location of related effects or downstream consequences when the charged district contains none of the proscribed conduct. The essential conduct in § 1519 is the act of “falsif[ying]” or “destroy[ing]” records; the intent “to impede, obstruct, or influence” a federal matter is a mens rea element that cannot by itself supply venue in a district where no falsification/destruction occurred, consistent with Article III and the Sixth Amendment’s vicinage guarantees. Allowing venue wherever an investigation is located would convert § 1519 into an effects/foreseeability venue regime untethered to where the crime was “committed,” inviting prosecutorial forum shopping absent a clear congressional statement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require that a crime be tried in the State and district where it was "committed," and our venue cases look to the statute’s essential conduct elements to identify that place. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519, the conduct Congress proscribed is the act of falsifying, destroying, or concealing records; the remaining language ("knowingly" and "with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence") supplies mens rea, not an additional conduct element occurring where an investigation happens to be located. Cabrales teaches that venue cannot be predicated on effects, related proceedings, or other circumstances untethered to the locus of the defendant’s criminal acts, and § 1519 notably does not require any obstruction to succeed—or even that an investigation already exist. Allowing venue where only the targeted investigation sits would convert venue into a foreseeability/effects test, inviting forum shopping and diluting the Constitution’s structural vicinage guarantees.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Constitution’s Venue and Vicinage guarantees (Art. III, § 2, cl. 3; Sixth Amendment) generally require that a federal crime be tried where it was committed, and when Congress has not specified venue the Court determines the locus delicti from the statute’s essential conduct elements and where those acts occurred. Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, § 1519’s essential conduct is the falsifying, destroying, or concealing of records; the “with the intent to” language is a mens rea element and does not itself supply venue in a district where no falsification/destruction occurred. Allowing venue solely in the district of the contemplated investigation would effectively convert venue into an effects/foreseeability rule and invite forum shopping, undermining the structural protections of Article III and the Sixth Amendment and creating practical workability and legitimacy concerns. Absent a clear congressional venue directive for § 1519, precedent and tradition counsel tying venue to where the defendant’s conduct occurred.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was “committed,” and our venue cases implement that guarantee by asking where the statute’s essential conduct elements occurred. Section 1519’s text criminalizes a defendant who “falsifies” or “destroys” a record “with the intent to impede” a federal matter; the operative conduct is the falsification/destruction, while the investigation’s location is at most a circumstance relevant to mens rea. Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue may not rest on intended effects or the locus of a targeted investigation when no proscribed conduct took place there. Because the alleged falsification occurred entirely in another district, venue in the investigation’s district would untether venue from the place of commission and invite the forum-shopping the Venue and Vicinage Clauses were designed to prevent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Because § 1519 contains no venue clause, Article III and the Sixth Amendment require venue where the crime was “committed,” which this Court determines by identifying the statute’s “essential conduct elements” and locating where that conduct occurred. Under Rodriguez-Moreno, mens rea or “circumstance” elements that are necessary for conviction do not themselves establish venue; for § 1519, the core conduct is the falsification/destruction/concealment of records, which (on these facts) occurred entirely in another district. Allowing venue solely where an investigation is located—based only on § 1519’s intent-to-obstruct language—risks diluting vicinage protections and invites forum shopping, undermining procedural fairness in a way the Venue Clauses are designed to prevent. The government can still prosecute obstruction, but it must do so in a district tethered to the defendant’s conduct (or under a statute with an express venue rule).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether venue for an 18 U.S.C. § 1519 prosecution may be laid in the district where the federal investigation was pending (and where the obstructive intent was directed) even if none of the defendant’s falsification conduct occurred there.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (falsification of records in federal investigations) and the Constitution’s venue requirements (U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 3; Sixth Amendment Vicinage Clause).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues venue is improper unless at least one essential conduct element of the charged offense occurred in the charging district. Because § 1519’s prohibited conduct is the act of falsifying/altering/destroying records, and that conduct occurred outside the district of prosecution, the government cannot rely on the statute’s intent element (i.e., intent to obstruct a federal investigation) and the investigation’s location to supply venue. Petitioner contends allowing venue wherever an investigation is located (or where contemplated effects might be felt) would unmoor venue from where the crime was committed, expand prosecutorial forum-shopping, and dilute the Article III/Sixth Amendment protections requiring trial in the place of the offense conduct.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues venue is proper in the district where the federal investigation was being conducted because the offense includes an intent to obstruct that investigation, and § 1519 is inherently directed at protecting the integrity of federal investigations. In the government’s view, where the investigation is located is a proper venue because that is where the obstructive conduct is aimed and where the criminal objective would be realized; thus the offense is sufficiently connected to that district even if the physical act of falsifying records happened elsewhere.
key_precedents: United States v. Percoco, 598 U.S. 319 (2023) (cert. granted sub nom. Ciminelli v. United States, 142 S. Ct. 2901 (2022))

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with Petitioner because the Constitution and our locus-delicti cases require venue to track § 1519’s essential conduct—“alter, destroy, conceal, falsify, or make a false entry”—and that conduct occurred only where the records were handled, not where investigators or a federal matter sit. The government’s strongest point is an effects/obstruction theory: that the statute is “about” interference with a federal investigation, so venue should follow the investigation’s district, but as Justice Kagan emphasizes via Cabrales, antecedent or related government activity in the charging district cannot substitute for out-of-district conduct that completes the offense. Justice Gorsuch’s distinction from Rodriguez-Moreno is also persuasive: there, kidnapping was itself an essential conduct element spanning districts, whereas § 1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” clause is mens rea/circumstance and cannot independently anchor venue. A narrow holding suffices: when all falsification (or other enumerated acts) occurs outside the charging district, venue may not rest solely on the location of a contemplated or pending federal matter absent an explicit statutory venue directive.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest conceivable argument for the government is that § 1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” language makes the federal matter’s situs part of the offense such that venue may follow the investigation, but that reads a mens rea/circumstance clause as an essential conduct element, contrary to the statute’s text. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito note, our Cabrales/Rodriguez-Moreno framework fixes venue on where the proscribed acts—“alter, destroy… falsify, or make a false entry”—occurred, not where the government later investigates or where the defendant hoped the obstruction would land. On an original public meaning understanding of Article III and the Sixth Amendment, venue must remain tethered to the locus delicti of the defendant’s conduct absent a clear congressional venue expansion, which § 1519 lacks. Because no falsification occurred in the charging district, venue there is unconstitutional and improper.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The government’s best point is the practical, obstruction-based claim that § 1519 should be “committed” where the contemplated federal matter or investigation sits because that is where the harm is felt, but that is an effects theory untethered to the statute’s essential conduct. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno require venue to track the locus of the conduct elements—here, the acts of falsifying/altering/destroying/concealing records—while the “in relation to or contemplation of” language functions as mens rea/circumstance and cannot, by itself, supply venue. Justice Kagan’s Cabrales analogy further underscores that an “anterior” federal connection in the charging district cannot substitute for out-of-district conduct that completes the offense. Absent a clear congressional venue expansion, adopting an investigation-situs rule would invite forum shopping and dilute Article III/Sixth Amendment vicinage protections, so I remain with Petitioner.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The government’s strongest pitch—that § 1519 is an obstruction statute whose venue should follow the situs of the federal matter or investigation—fails because it transforms a mens rea/circumstance clause (“in relation to or contemplation of”) into an essential conduct element, untethering venue from the defendant’s acts. Chief Justice Roberts’s conduct-based locus-delicti framing, reinforced by Justice Kagan’s Cabrales analogy, properly keeps venue where the falsification/alteration/destruction occurred rather than where investigators sit or where effects are later felt. From a pragmatic perspective attentive to access to justice, an investigation-situs rule would invite forum shopping and impose severe burdens on defendants with fewer resources, undermining the vicinage protections Article III and the Sixth Amendment were designed to secure. No colleague has identified a statutory text or precedent that squarely authorizes this kind of effects- or government-location venue expansion for § 1519, so I remain with Petitioner.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The government’s strongest point is the “obstruction” framing—that § 1519’s federal-matter nexus supplies a venue locus where the investigation or proceeding sits—but that treats an effects/object component as if it were an essential conduct element, which Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno do not permit. Chief Justice Roberts’s conduct-based locus delicti analysis is decisive under the constitutional venue clauses: the only conduct § 1519 prohibits is altering/destroying/concealing/falsifying records, so venue tracks where those acts occurred, not where investigators later worked. Justice Kavanaugh’s workability concern reinforces the textual and constitutional point: an investigation-situs rule would be a broad, atextual “government-location” venue provision that invites forum shopping absent a clear congressional directive. No colleague identified a precedent that undermines this conduct/mental-state distinction, so I remain with Petitioner.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The government’s best point—that § 1519 is an obstruction statute whose venue should follow the situs of the federal matter or investigation—still treats an intent/circumstance clause as an essential conduct element, which Cabrales forbids. Chief Justice Roberts is right that our venue cases identify the statute’s conduct verbs and locate where that conduct occurred; here, the only proscribed acts are “alter, destroy, conceal, [or] falsify,” and nothing in the “in relation to or contemplation of” language adds an act occurring where investigators sit. Rodriguez-Moreno doesn’t rescue the government because kidnapping there was itself an essential conduct element occurring in multiple districts, whereas § 1519’s investigation nexus is not conduct. Absent a clear congressional venue directive, adopting an investigation-situs theory would improperly dilute Article III and Sixth Amendment vicinage protections and invite forum shopping untethered to the defendant’s acts, as Justice Kagan’s Cabrales analogy underscores.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The government’s strongest argument—that § 1519 is an obstruction statute so venue should track the location of the federal matter/investigation—still misreads a mens rea/circumstance clause as an “essential conduct element,” which Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno do not permit. Chief Justice Roberts’s focus on the statute’s operative verbs (“falsify/alter/destroy/conceal”) properly identifies the locus delicti as the place where the defendant handled the records, not where agents later investigated or where the obstructive effects might be felt. Justice Kagan’s Cabrales analogy reinforces that an “anterior” federal connection in the charging district cannot substitute for out-of-district conduct that completes the offense, absent an explicit congressional venue expansion. For institutional and practical reasons, a conduct-based rule is also more administrable and better preserves Article III/Sixth Amendment vicinage protections against effects-based forum shopping.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention—that § 1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” language makes the federal matter’s situs an essential component for venue—still fails under our Cabrales/Rodriguez-Moreno framework because it converts a mens rea/circumstance clause into an essential conduct element. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Article III and the Sixth Amendment require tying venue to where the crime was “committed,” and here the only proscribed conduct is the alteration/destruction/falsification itself, not the location of investigators. Justice Gorsuch’s comparison to Rodriguez-Moreno confirms the distinction: there, kidnapping was itself conduct occurring in multiple districts, whereas § 1519’s investigation nexus does not require any act in the investigation’s district. Accepting an investigation-situs venue theory would produce an atextual, effects-based rule and invite forum shopping absent any clear congressional venue directive in § 1519’s text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The government’s strongest argument—that § 1519 is an obstruction statute whose venue should follow the location of the affected or contemplated federal matter—still fails under our essential-conduct framework. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Article III and the Sixth Amendment require anchoring venue to where the crime was “committed,” and under Cabrales/Rodriguez-Moreno that turns on the statute’s conduct verbs; here, the only proscribed acts are falsifying/altering/destroying/concealing records, not the government’s later investigation situs. Justice Kagan’s Cabrales analogy reinforces that an “anterior” federal connection in the charging district cannot substitute for in-district conduct absent a clear congressional venue expansion, which § 1519 lacks. From a pragmatic fairness perspective, adopting an investigation-location rule would invite strategic forum selection and impose asymmetric burdens on defendants in ways the vicinage protections were designed to prevent.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was “committed,” which this Court has tied to the location of the offense’s “essential conduct elements.” Under the two-step approach in United States v. Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, § 1519’s core conduct element is the act of falsifying/altering/destroying records; the investigation’s location and the defendant’s obstructive intent are circumstance/mental-state components that cannot alone supply venue. Allowing venue wherever an investigation is pending would dilute the Constitution’s venue protections and invite forum shopping, undermining institutional legitimacy, absent a clear congressional venue directive. Because none of the falsification conduct occurred in the charging district, venue there is improper.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III, § 2, cl. 3 and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was “committed,” which, as this Court has held, turns on where the offense’s essential conduct elements occurred, not where a related federal investigation was pending. Under § 1519’s text, the proscribed conduct is to “alter, destroy, mutilate, conceal, cover up, falsify, or make a false entry” in a record; the location of a federal investigation appears only in the mens rea (“in relation to or contemplation of” a federal matter) and does not create an additional conduct element. Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno instruct that venue cannot rest on the situs of governmental proceedings or anticipated effects when the charged conduct happened elsewhere; allowing venue wherever an investigation is located would detach venue from the place the defendant acted and invite forum-shopping inconsistent with the Constitution’s original meaning. Because none of the alleged falsification occurred in the charging district, venue there is improper.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require prosecution in the district where the crime was “committed,” which this Court has tied to the locus of the offense’s essential conduct elements rather than circumstance or intent elements. Under United States v. Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue turns on where the defendant’s proscribed acts occurred; for § 1519 the core conduct is “falsif[ying], alter[ing], destroy[ing]” records, and that conduct occurred only outside the charging district. Allowing venue to follow the location of a pending investigation would effectively convert § 1519 into an effects- or government-location venue rule untethered from where the defendant acted, inviting forum shopping and diluting the constitutional venue protections. Nothing in § 1519’s text purports to authorize such expanded venue, so the Constitution’s default rule controls.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require prosecution where the crime was “committed,” which this Court has tied to the location of the offense’s essential conduct elements rather than downstream effects or related proceedings. Under the two-step approach reflected in United States v. Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, § 1519’s core conduct is falsifying/altering/destroying records; the investigation-obstruction intent describes purpose, not additional conduct that can independently anchor venue. Allowing venue wherever an investigation is pending would dilute vicinage protections and invite forum shopping, imposing practical burdens on defendants—especially those least able to travel or litigate far from home—that the Venue and Vicinage Clauses were designed to prevent. Because none of the falsification conduct occurred in the charging district, venue there is improper absent a clear congressional directive expanding venue beyond the locus delicti.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require venue where the crime was committed, and under the Cabrales/Rodriguez-Moreno framework we identify the statute’s essential conduct elements and locate where that conduct occurred. Section 1519’s proscribed conduct is to “alter, destroy, mutilate, conceal, cover up, falsify, or make a false entry” in a record; the location of a federal investigation is at most a circumstance tied to the statute’s intent requirement (“in relation to or contemplation of” a federal matter), not conduct that can itself supply venue. As in United States v. Cabrales, where the “anterior” Missouri drug activity could not establish venue for Florida money-laundering transactions, the investigation’s situs cannot establish venue for out-of-district falsification. Allowing venue wherever an investigation is pending would expand prosecutorial choice in a way unmoored from the statute’s conduct and in tension with constitutional venue protections absent a clear congressional directive.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was committed, and our cases instruct that venue ordinarily turns on the location of the offense’s essential conduct elements, not on where intended effects might be felt. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519, the only essential conduct element is the act of falsifying/altering/destroying a record; the remaining components ("knowingly" and "with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence") are mens rea and cannot, standing alone, supply venue in a district where no falsification occurred. As in Cabrales, where money-laundering venue could not be laid where the underlying drug crime occurred absent laundering conduct there, the government may not anchor venue to the situs of a federal investigation when the charged falsification conduct took place entirely elsewhere. Permitting venue wherever an investigation is pending would dilute the Constitution’s venue safeguards and invite forum-shopping untethered to the statute’s text and the locus delicti of the criminal act.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Because § 1519 contains no special venue provision, venue must satisfy Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment by lying where the crime was committed, determined by identifying the statute’s “essential conduct elements” and locating where that conduct occurred. Under the Cabrales/Rodriguez-Moreno framework, § 1519’s essential conduct is the act of “falsif[ying],” “alter[ing],” “destroy[ing],” or “conceal[ing]” a record, while the intent to impede a federal investigation is a circumstance/mental-state element that does not itself create venue. Allowing venue solely where an investigation is pending would detach venue from the defendant’s conduct, invite forum-shopping, and undermine the Constitution’s vicinage protections. Practical workability also favors a clear conduct-based rule: prosecutors can charge where falsification occurred (or where the statute expressly permits), rather than litigating investigative “targets” and effects.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was “committed,” which this Court has implemented by asking (1) what the offense’s essential conduct elements are and (2) where that conduct occurred. Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue turns on the location of the conduct constituting the offense, not on the place where downstream effects are felt or where related proceedings occur. The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1519 criminalizes the act of “alter[ing], destroy[ing], mutilat[ing], conceal[ing], cover[ing] up, falsif[ying], or mak[ing] a false entry” in a record; the investigation-related language supplies the mens rea/object, not an additional conduct element occurring where the investigation sits. Because no falsification conduct occurred in the charging district, laying venue there based solely on the investigation’s location would dilute constitutional venue protections and invite forum shopping absent clear statutory authorization.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Constitution’s venue guarantees (Art. III, § 2, cl. 3; Sixth Amendment) require trial in the district where the offense was committed, which this Court has implemented by identifying the statute’s essential conduct elements and locating where that conduct occurred. Under Rodriguez-Moreno and Cabrales, venue generally lies where the defendant’s proscribed conduct took place, not merely where the intended effects would be felt; here, § 1519’s essential conduct is “knowingly… falsif[ying]… any… document,” and the investigation-directed intent does not itself supply a conduct locus. Allowing venue wherever an investigation is pending would dilute vicinage protections and invite forum shopping, with serious practical consequences for defendants—concerns that weigh heavily in ensuring procedural fairness in criminal prosecutions. Because none of the falsification conduct occurred in the charging district, venue cannot rest solely on the investigation’s location or the defendant’s obstructive intent.
